56.t: Bolden and Robichaux competing at Lincoln Park
56.s: Bolden's band played the skating rink while Robichaux played the pavilion, drawing the crowd with a horn out the window.
56.ch: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
56.q: And finished telling you, before I started playing there, you know. Yeah. When I used to go from Laplace, you know. Yes. Robichoux used to play every Sunday, afternoon, Sunday night. Uh huh. But the Bowling would play out, well, Malling Bird or Milling Bird, they called it then. Yeah. And that…

56.t: What Bolden looked like and how he practiced
56.s: Ory describes Bolden's hair, build and loud practising on the sidewalk step.
56.ch: Bolden and the road to New Orleans
56.q: Yeah, he was kind of on a Moroni style look, you know. His hair went black and more exactly red. I see. Red and... And black. And they never combed it, it was always just way out of a cutty loose there. Was he big or small? Well, it's the time I saw him then, he was the size of, I say, Jim…

56.t: Bolden's playing and what Ory thought of it
56.s: Bolden was rough and loud with no tone but deserves credit.
56.ch: Lincoln Park and the name Kid
56.q: Yeah, but we hadn't been a conception, you know, tone and stuff. Bolden was very rough, you see. You have to give him credit for starting the ball rolling, you know. Yeah. But he wasn't really a musician. Who, Bolden? He didn't study. I mean, he was gifted. Yeah. I mean, playing, you know, would…

771.t: Buddy Bolden: his playing, his band and the Eagle Band
771.s: Bocage recalls Bolden as a loud blues player, lists his sidemen, says Duson took over the band as the Eagle Band, and describes their keys and tempos.
771.q: I remember Buddy. I was quite young though. He died young too. He was an old fellow when he died. He must have been in his thirties, you know? What kind of trumpet playing did you make? Well he was mostly a blues player, you know? Mostly blues. He mostly make tunes, you know, like a pallet on the…

771.t: Hearing Buddy Bolden and comparing trumpeters
771.s: He heard Bolden once around 1906-07, describes his power and how the fast life broke him, and compares him to Keppard.
771.q: I heard him once, yes. I was a kid. I was just fixing to start out, you know, man. I was just fixing to go out and start playing. And he played over here once and I heard him play. Well, like I told you, he died a young man, you know. He wasn't old.

181.s: Parker recalls Buddy Bolden playing loud at Lincoln Park and the dancing there; mentions balloon ascents.
181.q: you didn't get did you go to the parks did you ever go to the parks sure man sure I went to the park Lincoln Park that's what Buddy Bolton used to play all the time question for you yes indeed Buddy Bolton getting right across from the park what's that other Johnson Park up there yeah that's right…

181.s: Parker recalls trumpeter Edward Clem and Buddy Bolden as blues king, reading and playing at Dixie Park.
181.q: This fella, Reed, he brought you Norm Good, too. I seen his name in the book yesterday, uh... Edward Clem. You know Edward Clem.

2.t: Bolden: contradictory information and the cylinder
2.s: Russell resumes on Buddy Bolden, the lack of reliable facts and the disputed Bolden cylinder.
2.q: We were talking about Bolden and the fact that there's so little real information and so much contradictory information, and he is such a key figure to the whole New Orleans scene. He's such a famous, legendary character that, of course, as I say, I don't think it's necessary to have to defend our…

2.t: Minor Hall's death; Jazzmen errors and Bolden doubts
2.s: Russell notes Minor Hall's death, the errors in Jazzmen, and doubts about Bolden's existence and the photograph.
2.q: Yeah, no, Minor died. We got a good interview with him in 1958. Wow. He was playing very little then. He had left the Ori band in a disagreement.

21.t: Bolden's playing style and the Panama rags
21.s: Bolden played mostly straight music loudly, could read, and was heard across the river.
21.q: Well, I'll tell you, how Buddy played, Buddy played straight music mostly, but loud. The only random music I hear Buddy played was like blues, pallet on the flow, and them kind of things.

21.s: He lists the men in Bolden's band, how Dusen joined, and remembers hearing them at Funky Butt.
21.q: What did I hear them play? I had a place on Padilla Street, on this side of the place, used to call it Funky Buddy. I came over and played with my brother. All you could hear once. During that time, the gloves were all around him. Got a place out here. Out by the base, the gloves. Where the…

46.t: Buddy Bolden and the balloon advertisement at Lincoln Park
46.s: He recalls Bolden playing from a wagon to advertise Lincoln Park, with a balloon ascension, and breaking down.
46.ch: Hightower: New Orleans parades and early players
46.q: Just enough to know that about, I don't know how long it was, but just about the time I got, I wasn't old enough to play then, see. Yeah. I played at a place called the Lincoln Park. That's around Carlton Avenue. Yeah. It used to have Buddy Bolden, used to go up in a balloon. Man used to go up in a…

46.t: Bunk Johnson as a boy and Buddy Bolden's band
46.s: Hightower says Bunk began playing with Bolden's band as a child, living in his neighborhood.
46.ch: Hightower: New Orleans parades and early players
46.q: Oh, yes. But I was so small then, see. And his mother didn't want him to play. So Bolden and them begged his mother and they took him on a job. And Bolden used to bring his clothes for him to dress him. And take him back home and put him in his knee pants and send him home. He lived in my…

633.t: Hearing Buddy Bolden at Congo Square on a visit
633.s: Bolden was on his way out; he heard him and other bands outside Globe Hall at the square.
633.q: Not that I know of. Bolden was on his way out when I got here. I heard him several times. He used to go around by the... He used to have a square right where the auditorium is now. That square that used to go straight across, used to be named Congo Square, the changes to Burgard Square. And they…

633.s: Barnes cannot name Bolden's unnamed tunes; Bolden was passing out when he arrived.
633.q: Well, I couldn't think of all of them because it didn't have no name, you know? It didn't have no name.

650.t: Buddy Bolden: loudest trumpeter, hall player, poisoned trumpet story
650.s: Bolden was a very loud, popular hall player who never worked the district; Amacker has heard he died from a poisoned trumpet.
650.q: Yeah, he's, he's the loudest trumpet player. He, well, there's some, some pieces he played was, was very popular, you know. It was very popular in that day. I wouldn't say the name for that lady.

650.t: Buddy Bolden's repertoire and 'The House Got Ready'
650.s: Bolden played old blues; Amacker recalls tunes like Funky Butt and The House Got Ready, which got dancers wild.
650.q: Oh this old old iron blues stuff like that. You remember any of them? Well you see the old old iron blues he played. On the piano I did but not on this guitar. On the piano I know some.

172.t: Bolden's band size, instruments and playing
172.s: Bolden at Johnson Park versus Robichaux at Lincoln Park; bands of four to six; Bolden was loud and strong.
172.q: That's when we used to have Buddy Bowling playing what's called Johnson Park and Robichaud playing and Lincoln Park. There was about four blocks separating each other, you see. So that's where I know both of those from. I used to visit those places, but I would live in Indiana. I was a boy.

179.t: Buddy Bolden known only by talk
179.s: Bocage never heard Buddy Bolden but heard much talk of him; Dick relays what Fess told him.
179.q: Well, uh, the old Masonic Hall they had here at that time, uh, that was the second horse hall, that was down here on Ballette Street.

567.t: Ringing the bell, old musicians and Buddy Bolin
567.s: White says he still rings the bell and meets old musicians; Allen asks about Buddy Bolin, whose death followed the killing of Chief Anderson, and the old workhouse site.
567.ch: Second lining and the brass bands
567.q: The church and everything. That's what he wants to know. Well, I don't talk about all them new, all them old times. I don't talk about all that. All them music parts. I know all that. Music, all them music parts. I know all that.

246.t: More on Buddy Bolden, and Bigfoot Willis the flute player
246.s: Asked about Bolden's band, Glass says he knew them only by sight; Bolden worked regularly and Glass was not around when he was taken away. Glass also describes Bigfoot Willis, a tall flutist in a cape on Decatur Street.
246.q: No, I didn't play with Buddy Bowling. I didn't play with him. Cause they had their line up. They played. And you knew the guys in his band? Did you know any of them? I just know them by seeing them, you know, the part being friends with them like that,

430.t: Hearing Buddy Bolden blow as a tiny child
430.s: He recalls his mother saying Buddy Bolden blew too loud at banquets at the hall behind their home.
430.q: Well, I tell you, I heard him, but I didn't see him and my mama told me we was living in the back of Police of Burns Hall. We lived on the airport street and Police of Burns Hall happened to be on Village Street and we lived in the back of Police of Burns Hall and every Monday used to have a lot of…

254.t: Bolden's decline and how his music differed from Robichaux's
254.s: He recalls Bolden going crazy, and says the Bolden band played rough music unlike Robichaux's, and the two were not hired by the same club on one night.
254.q: Yeah. He didn't know you used to play around the band. I was like, fuck, they used to play all over. You were going to just play. Mm-hmm. But they used to play all of the little halls downtown. They had better little halls, little clubs and things all downtown. What was the difference between the…

184.t: Walter Brundy, Buddy Bolden and the drummers he never knew
184.s: Hall remembers Walter Brundy, doesn't recall other old drummers, and saw Buddy Bolden once at Lincoln Park.
184.ch: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
184.q: See, another day that I remember, Walter Brundy and the Zeno, while old man Contrell and now let's see, I can remember. Old timers. No, that's... Remember Mac Murray? No, I don't, no. I've heard of him, but I don't remember him.

773.t: Buddy Petit and Big Eye; Olympia band at the auditorium
773.s: Buddy Petit played with her husband; Big Eye as a young player; the Olympia band was the first black band at the auditorium.
773.q: Oh, yeah, all of them. Buddy Petit was great, too. He was a good player. He had a funeral when he died. You know Armstrong came in, especially with him. He had a big funeral. Buddy Petit, oh, that was all... He was another fellow who drank hard, but he played. You could say he died young. And, oh,…

620.t: Hearing Buddy Bolden's band at West End
620.s: He remembers Bolden's band from about age seven, hearing it at West End, plus Charlie Charlie playing piano there.
620.q: Piano player, yeah. I heard him, the first place I ever heard him playing outside of a house was out there at the West End Tavis. Out there on the Pulse Train Boulevard back then. That was years ago, though. Not right, not lately. An old man out there.

23.t: Trip to see Buddy Bolden at the Jackson state hospital
23.s: Rose recalls, aged twelve, going with his uncle to the Louisiana state hospital where Bolden took a cornet, examined it and handed it back without recognition.
23.q: I can't really tell you the answer to that. I know that he was involved with musicians a great deal, and, uh, I do know that he had some project afoot where he was considering doing some kind of recording, but, uh, actually, I was not very clear on the subject at the time. You know, kids, uh, don't…

12.t: Hearing Buddy Bolden as a child
12.s: He heard Bolden at Lincoln Park as a young boy, was unimpressed, and doubts the legend built around him.
12.q: Well, I've had the pleasure to hear Buddy Bolden when I was a young lad, around seven, eight, six years old, something like that, the first time. He was playing at the Lincoln Park uptown. My Uncle Joe used to take me up there on Sundays. It was a matinee thing in the open air. And I've heard him…

590.t: Buddy Bolden's fate and Armstrong's fame in Alcorn's youth
590.s: Alcorn recalls Bolden losing his mind and being forgotten, while everybody in his time talked about Louis Armstrong.
590.ch: Lil, Oliver and the Hot Five
590.q: Oh, yeah. So Buddy Bolden died, I was pretty young when he died, because they brought him back here. My mother didn't know Buddy Bolden.

188.s: He remembers Bolden's rough band at Johnson Park beside Robichaux at Lincoln Park, and the mud on Carrollton Avenue.
188.q: Yes, sir. He used to play at Lincoln Park. Buddy Bolden played at Lincoln... at Johnson Park and Robichaux played at Lincoln Park. It was right joining. Yeah.

182.t: Buddy Bolden's band and how he played
182.s: He remembers the loud ragtime and blues of the Bolden band and watching it as a boy with his mouth open.
182.q: Oh yeah, oh yeah, it was ragtime, that was ragtime, ragtime, ragtime, you know, all them blues and everything like that. Loud, you could hear him. Four o'clock in the morning, you could hear him cross the road. Yeah, yeah. It was just loud, you know, playing like, didn't care, you know. Just didn't…

777.t: Buddy Bolden as a strong trumpet player
777.s: Williams heard Buddy Bolden around 1905-06 and describes him as a strong trumpet player who played at halls; he visited the city since 1902.
777.ch: Early New Orleans music and Mardi Gras
777.q: Buddy Bolin, I was quite young when he played. That might be around 1905 or 1906. But I heard him play it several times. He was a strong trumpet player. He was a strong trumpet player. He had that Jackson Street Hall, Long Termin Hall, and he hadn't played well at that Lincoln Park. You know he…

8.t: Playing with Buddy Bolden at Kenner's Hall
8.s: Garland subbed on bass for Little Jimmy at Liberty and Perdido and names Bolden's lineup: Willie Cornish, Frank Lewis, Brock Mumford and James Phillip.
8.ch: Serenading and playing with Buddy Bolden
8.q: Then the band consisted of Jimmy Adyazin on the bass. Carnish, Willie Carnish was on trombone. Frank, I forget Frank's last name, played clarinet. The guy from across the lake? And then Brock played guitar. James E. Phillip played drums. That's way back now you don't talk about.

830.t: Buddy Bolden: not played with, but his family known
830.s: George did not play with Bolden, but she knew his mother and sister and says he lost his mind; she was not allowed to go to dances as a girl.
830.ch: Learning music and the early bands
830.q: But, um, I don't think he played music too very long when he took sick of all the time. Yeah, she lost his mind. Yeah, he lost his mind.

55.t: Buddy Bolden's loud trumpet and Carnish
55.s: Bolden's volume and style, Carnish on trombone, and instruments left in the pool room.
55.q: You understand? About to jump out with him, you know? That's why these guys in the prison all of them talking about. They're there with papas. Tony, I'm a Rick and all of them.

198.s: Dick Allen asks how Funky Butt went; Barnes cannot recall it.
198.q: Buddy Variant, that was him in there. I was trying to play the drums on the Amite, you see, and kind of be burrowing in there.

127.t: Wanting to have heard Buddy Bolden; photographs
127.s: Punch regrets never seeing Buddy Bolden, whom people said drew dancers; the interviewers then talk about taking a good picture.
127.q: Buddy Bowden Everybody told me how he could play on on uh Third and Willow and the people that Howard Avenue and Ramport be dancing by his music Were there stuff stuff Were there stuff ! ! ! ! ! ! ! ! And the people would enjoy him at Howard Avenue and Ramport would be dancing by the music. Boy,…

128.t: Magnolia plantation band and its dead members
128.s: He heard the Magnolia band as a boy; most of the old players, such as trumpeter Riffith Harrison Bones, are dead.
128.q: Oh, well, I'll tell you, a lot of them people is dead. I couldn't remember all them people's names. I just thought you could tell us- But Sonny could tell you all them fellas' names, because he used to play in that band with him,
